newsitem.title: KENYA: US aid worker escapes kidnap in Somalia.
newsitem.headline: US aid worker escapes kidnap in Somalia.

text.p: An American aid worker with the U.S. Agency for International Development has escaped after being kidnapped in Somalia, a U.S. embassy spokesman said on Monday.

Californian Daniel Suther, 30, who was monitoring food distribution for a non-governmental organisation, was kidnapped last Friday after renting a vehicle in Belet-Huen 260 km (160 miles) north of the capital Mogadishu.
He managed to escape the same day after jumping out of the vehicle and was flown back to Nairobi on Sunday, the Nairobi embassy spokesman said.

"He (Suther and the kidnappers) was on a one-lane road and three trucks were coming in the opposite direction, so the vehicle pulled off the road and as the first truck went by he got out, ran across the road and took off into the bush and kept going," the spokesman said.
The kidnappers, who forced other passengers out of the vehicle to effect the kidnap, apparently fired no shots and Suther spent the night under a tree.
On Saturday he continued walking and in the afternoon met a camel rider who gave him water and tea.
Later he met a vehicle sent to look for him and returned to Belet-Huen before being flown out on Sunday morning.
Suther, a veteran of Somalia has already been kidnapped once in the country, the spokesman said without giving further details.
Somalia has been without central government since 1991 when late president Siad Barre was ousted. Hundreds of thousands died in 1992/93 during a famine fueled by civil war.
The spokesman said Suther's kidnappers were associated with south Mogadishu faction leader Hussein Aideed.
Militia loyal to Hussein Aideed's father Mohamed Farah Aideed fought U.S. and United Nations troops in Somalia under the banner of Operation Restore Hope during the famine.
In another development Italian Minister of State for Foreign Affairs Rino Serri said in Nairobi the international community was concerned Somalia was becoming a centre for political violence.
"It's been confirmed that so-called Afghan groups are in Somalia and it is possible the country could become and in some aspects has become a center for terrorism," Serri told reporters.
"And this is a danger the whole international community is aware of -- including many Arab countries. That's why there should be a strong push to find a solution to Somalia," he said.
Serri is due to make a one-day trip to Mogadishu on Tuesday where he hopes to meet Hussein Aideed and north Mogadishu faction leader Ali Mahdi Mohamed.
Serri declined to comment on an inquiry into alleged atrocities committed by Italians in Somalia during Operation Restore Hope.
